reason: Wrong part. The examples describe auricles, scales and rhizome scales, not trichomes. The part comes from a bad bearer match.
Stolons can spread or grow outward. The examples fit.
A leaf sheath margin can have a colour (black, brown, pale brown). The examples are correct.

Wrong reading. 'Continuous or interrupted' says whether the indusium forms an unbroken ring. It does not say whether the indusium is present, which is what 'occurrence' means. A continuity rule is needed.
Wrong reading. 'Angled obliquely upward' or 'acroscopically' gives the insertion angle or direction of the pinna. The pinna is not bent. Orientation or angle is the right quality.
A bulb can be subcylindrical.
Tepal apices can be retuse.
A synandrium (fused androecium) is a round or discoid structure, and its diameter is given in mm.
A fruit pedicel can be dilated, usually at the apex.
A pseudostaminode can be oblong.
Pseudobulbs are often clavate. The examples are correct.
A leaf lamina lobe can be notched at the apex or margin.
An orchid labellum can be cuneate.
A spathe can be concave.
'Pale' is low colour saturation, and a scale leaf (cataphyll) can be pale. Some examples carry a hue as well, which a colour rule should split off.
A ligule can be rigid or stiff. A few examples are about hairs on the ligule, not the ligule itself.
Leaf sheath auricles can be clasping (amplexicaul).
Floral disc lobes have shapes such as semiorbicular, ovoid and conic. The apex fragments (retuse, mucronate) belong to apex shape, not this pair.
The examples mix an awn on the apex that falls off with the whole leaf apex falling off as a propagule. A rule would need to know which part falls off, and the awn would then be the bearer.
A perispore can have ridges (lophate). The 'without ridges' example needs a negation check.
Pinnules can be ascending, spreading or descending.
A floral disc, or its lobes, can be obconical. The lobes also have their own class.
A floral disc can be divided or dissected into lobes. The example 'each divided by a septum' is about the ovary and should not be counted.
A leaf can bear nodules or be nodular on its surface.
A petal apex can be toothed or dentate.
A spadix appendix has a width, given as 'length × width' or 'larges de ...'.
A tuber or tuberoid can be small.
A spathe tube can be cylindrical.
A fruit can be sessile or subsessile. The PO class is a utricle, a one-seeded fruit that is not a capsule, but the pair is fine.
A calyx tube has a width. 'Long et de large' gives length and width together, which a dimension rule should split.
A leaf can be subtriangular. 'Furrow subtriangular' is a different part.
An anther connective can be strap- or tongue-shaped.
A cladode (phylloclade) is flat.
A keel can be fimbriate, and so can its appendages.
A pinna or its base can be symmetrical or asymmetrical.
Wrong reading. 'Solitary' for an embryo means one embryo (a count, as in polyembryony), not a spatial pattern. It belongs to the count pattern.
A lamina lobe can be ovate, oblong or deltoid.
The base of a plant organ can be truncate.
Internodes can be curved or arcuate.
A prophyll can be keeled. The keel count ('2-keeled') should go to the count pattern.
A lodicule can be elliptic.
A lodicule can be thickened or thick, often at the base.
A caryopsis can be obovoid.
A fruit can be subtriangular or subtrigonous. The 'abaxial wing' example is another part.
A capsule can be clavate.
A floral corona can be reduced in size. The value is 'reduced', so the pair should map to the small or reduced size value.
An ovary can be subulate.
An anther can be bent or geniculate.
An ovule can be obovoid, ovoid or ellipsoid.
A frond can be lanceolate.
A glume can be fringed, usually along the margin with hairs.
A corolla lobe can be crenulate or scalloped at the margin.
An inflorescence axis such as a rachilla can be conspicuous or visible.
Part of the examples (strongly geniculate near base) describe the awn, not the lemma. 'Angled margins' is an angle, not a bend. A rule would need to know whether the lemma body or the awn is bent.
A gynostemium (orchid column) can be subcylindrical.
A stylopodium can be disc-shaped.
A floral disc can be spotted with dots.
A gynostemium can be glabrous.
A labellum lobe margin can be fimbriate.
A legume can be ovoid or obovoid.
